en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhi of Changshui, Part Two:
The Sixfold Reciprocal Retribution. Section One: General Summary.
"What are the six retributions? Ānanda! All sentient beings create karma through their six consciousnesses; the evil [retribution] they thereby attract..."
"Retribution issues forth from the six sense organs.

Since the creation of karma originates from the six sense organs, the experience of retribution returns to the six sense organs; because cause and effect intersect, it is called "intersecting retribution" (jiaobao).
Furthermore, when one faculty undergoes retribution, all six faculties experience it in succession; since this occurs for every faculty, it is called "mutual retribution" (*jiaobao*).
As for the statement that the six consciousnesses create karma, this refers merely to their general characteristics.
"Karma" (karma) has the meaning of "invoking and inducing. It applies both generally and specifically.

If it functions as a projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), wherein wholesome or unwholesome volition (*cetanā*) invokes the future eighth [consciousness], which is neutral (*avyākṛta*), this is "general retributive karma.

If it functions as a completing karma (*paripūrakakarman*), wherein seeds of volition of the three natures invoke future fruits such as suffering or pleasure, this is called "specific retributive karma."
The sixth consciousness can produce both collective and individual retributive karma;

whereas the first five consciousnesses merely assist in producing individual retribution and cannot produce collective retribution, due to the two distinctions of being "powerful" (*balavat*) and "conforming" (*anuvartaka*).

Regarding that which issues from the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*): since the six sense faculties are the instruments by which one creates karma, and since the creation [of karma] proceeds from the faculties, its reception is likewise received by the faculties; therefore, it issues from the faculties.
II. Detailed Analysis, in six parts: I.
Seeing the Retribution, in two parts: A.
Seeing the Objects at the Time of Death.
"How do evil retributions emerge from the six sense organs?
First is the retribution of sight, which draws forth evil fruits.

When this visual karma intersects with other karmas, at the time of death one first sees fierce fires filling the ten directions. The deceased’s consciousness flies downward, riding upon the smoke, and enters the Avīci Hell, manifesting two distinct appearances: [...]"
The eye-faculty committing offenses is the karma of seeing; the vision of objects at the moment of death is the intersection of retribution and karma.
Because the eye-faculty grasps forms and these forms can enslave the mind, one commits various kinds of karma; therefore, one sees fierce fires filling the ten directions.
The consciousness follows the fire into hell to undergo retribution.
Second, receiving retribution according to one's karma:
"First is clear vision; one can then see all manner of evil things and give rise to immeasurable fear."
Second is dark vision: seeing nothing in the profound stillness, one gives rise to immeasurable fear.
Seeing fire in this way, it can burn the ears into boiling cauldrons and molten copper;
it can burn the breath into black smoke and purple flames.
The burning of flavors can produce scorched balls and molten iron;
the burning of touch can produce hot ashes and furnace coals;
the burning of the mind can give rise to sparks that scatter and fly about, fanning and filling the void.

The two objects of light and darkness are what is apprehended by the eye; because light can be discerned, one perceives its negative aspects, whereas darkness lacks such discrimination and merely gives rise to fear.

In this manner, one proceeds downward through all six sense faculties. However, there is a distinction between the primary and the secondary; since it is primarily through the eye faculty that consciousness is generated and karma is created, the eye is traversed first.
That this is not explicitly stated here is merely due to the brevity of the text, as the details are fully provided in the subsequent passage.

In this context, fire serves as the primary instrument of suffering; furthermore, as it passes through the other sense faculties, it transforms according to each faculty into objects that are disagreeable to the mind.
Second, the retribution of hearing has two parts:
first, the vision of objects at the time of death.
"Second is the retribution of hearing, which draws forth evil fruits.

When this karma of hearing intersects with other conditions, at the time of death one first perceives waves and surges that submerge heaven and earth; the deceased's consciousness descends and flows along with them, entering the Avīci Hell, manifesting two appearances:
sound can agitate the ocean of the mind, appearing like waves and surges."
Because one performs karma by grasping these [objects], one perceives them first at the time of death.
"Descending and pouring" refers to flowing downward.
Second, receiving retribution through the power of karma.
"First is 'listening with the doors open,' wherein one hears various clamors and the spirit becomes muddled and disordered;
second is 'listening with the doors closed,' wherein there is silence and nothing is heard, causing the dark soul to sink into oblivion."
Thus, when the waves of hearing strike the ears, they can act as reproach and interrogation;
when they strike the eyes, they can act as thunder, as roars, and as noxious poisonous vapors;
when they strike the breath, they can act as rain and mist, sprinkling all manner of venomous insects that cover the entire body.
If one pours it upon flavor, it becomes pus, blood, and various kinds of filth;
if poured upon touch, it becomes beasts, ghosts, excrement, and urine;
if poured upon thought, it becomes lightning and hail that shatter the heart and soul.
The two objects—movement and stillness—apprehended by the faculty of hearing create various karmas; now, one receives their retribution, which likewise depends on these two.
Opening [the ears] is movement; closing them is stillness.
In this manner, one proceeds downward through the distinct faculties and their respective experiences.

Within this passage, there appear discrepancies in the correlation between the faculties and their objects; it is feared that the Sanskrit original may have been transposed, and the translator followed it without careful scrutiny.

The roar of thunder and poisonous vapors are not objects apprehended by the eye; rain, mist, and venomous insects are not within the domain of the nose. The remainder of the text follows accordingly; those with wisdom may examine it for themselves.
Third, the retribution of smelling, which has two parts:
first, encountering objects at the moment of death.
"Third is the retribution of smelling, which summons and brings about evil fruits."

When this smelling karma intersects with other karmas, at the time of death, one first sees poisonous vapors filling the near and far surroundings. The deceased’s consciousness surges up from the earth and enters the Avīci Hell, manifesting two signs:

because the faculty of the nose committed offenses by greedily smelling various fragrances—the scents of sentient beings’ bodies, men, women, and so forth—and performed various kinds of karma, it thus summons poisonous vapors to undergo its retribution.
Second, the retribution for the karma of the vehicles.
"First is 'obstructed hearing,' where one is permeated by various evil vapors, causing extreme mental agitation;
second is 'blocked hearing,' where the vapors overwhelm and obstruct the senses, leading to fainting on the ground."
When smelling odors in this way, if they strike the breath, they can become solid matter or footwear;
if they strike the sight, they can become fire or torches;
if they strike the hearing, they can become submergence, drowning, melting, or boiling.
When it strikes the sense of taste, it can manifest as hunger or a refreshing coolness;
when it strikes the sense of touch, it can manifest as bursting, rotting, or vast mountains of flesh with hundreds of thousands of eyes and immeasurable mouths for devouring;
when it strikes the mind, it can manifest as ashes, miasma, or flying sand and gravel that shatter the body.
"Permeability and obstruction are the objects apprehended by that nose; based upon these, one performs karma and based upon these, one undergoes suffering; therefore, there are two aspects.
In this manner, one proceeds through the lower sense faculties, each experiencing its own particularity."
"To be 'obstructed' (zhi) and to be 'traversable' (li): obstruction refers to physical resistance; traversability refers to what is still passable.
To be 'putrid' (nai) and to be 'discordant' (shuang): when fish spoil, they become putrid.
Discordance refers to deviation and error."
The remaining text may be understood.
Fourth, the retribution experienced while alive has two parts:
first, the visions encountered at the time of death.
"Fourth is the retribution of flavor, which draws forth evil fruits.

When this karmic activity of flavor intersects with other factors, at the moment of death one first sees an iron net and fierce, blazing flames that completely envelop the world. The deceased’s consciousness passes downward through them, hanging upside down from the net, its head entering the Avīci Hell, where two signs manifest:
the tongue-root commits offenses that are the most extensive of all."
First, indulging in the craving for flavors constitutes a transgression that inevitably leads to much slaughter;

second, the karma produced by verbal expression is even more extensive. When compared to the other faculties, false speech, frivolous talk, divisive speech, and harsh words are the most widespread; therefore, they result in the world being completely covered by an iron net.
Second, the retribution received through the karma of the vehicle:
"First, the inhaled breath solidifies into freezing ice, which freezes and tears the flesh of the body;
second, the exhaled breath flies forth as fierce fire, which scorches and rots the marrow and bones."
Tasting flavors in this manner, through repeated tasting, one becomes capable of receiving and enduring;
through repeated seeing, one becomes capable of melting metal and stone;
through repeated hearing, one becomes capable of wielding sharp weapons.
When it passes through the breath, it can become a great iron cage covering the entire land;
when it passes through the sense of touch, it can become bows, arrows, crossbows, and projectiles;
when it passes through thought, it can become flying red-hot iron falling from the sky.
"Inhalation draws in the flavors [of food], while exhalation results in the utterance of speech.
Thus, one experiences the various sensations through each sense organ in succession.
To 'bear' and to 'endure' means to receive and patiently accept all unpleasant tastes."

At the time of creating karma, first the tongue-faculty receives food and perceives its flavor; only then do the great elements of the other faculties receive nourishment. If the tongue does not perceive flavor, the other faculties are not nourished; the same applies to the receiving of retribution.
Five, the retribution of touch, has two parts:
first, the vision of objects at the moment of death.
"The fifth is the retribution of touch, which draws forth evil fruits."

When this contact and karma intersect, at the time of death, one first sees great mountains closing in from all four sides with no way out. The deceased’s consciousness perceives a great iron city, where fire-snakes, fire-dogs, tigers, wolves, lions, ox-headed hell-wardens, and horse-headed rākṣasas, holding spears and halberds in their hands, drive them through the city gates toward the Avīci Hell. This manifests two aspects:

because the body-faculty, due to many offenses, was involved in the contact of sexual desire between men and women, craving smoothness and softness, and experiencing cold and heat according to the season, one consequently undergoes the experience of the closing mountains and other such events.
Second, the retribution received through the karma of the vehicle:
"First is contact by conjunction, where mountains close in upon the body, crushing the bones, flesh, and blood;
second is contact by separation, where swords and blades strike the body, tearing the heart and liver asunder."
In this way, when combined with contact, as it passes through touch, it can serve as a path, an observation, a hall, or a table;
when passing through seeing, it can serve as burning or heat;
when passing through hearing, it can serve as a clashing, a striking, an impaling, or a shooting.
When experienced through the breath, it can become a hook, a bag, a test, or a bond;
when experienced through the sense of taste, it can become plowing, tongs, cutting, or slicing;
when experienced through thought, it can become falling, flying, frying, or roasting.
"What the body perceives consists only of contact and separation; from these one commits offenses, and the resulting retribution is likewise.
Thus, one proceeds downward through the various sense organs to receive [retribution].
The 'Path,' the 'Observation,' the 'Hall,' and the 'Table' are all places for punishing offenses."
The remaining text is easily understood.
Six: The Retribution of Thought, in two parts:
First, the visions seen at the time of death.
"Sixth is the retribution of volition, which draws forth and invites evil fruits.

When this volitional karma intersects [with other conditions], at the time of death one first sees an evil wind blowing away and destroying the land. The deceased's spirit-consciousness is blown upward into the air, then whirled down with the wind and falls into the Avīci Hell, manifesting two appearances:
Volition is mental karma; it is without substance and swift as the wind, and thus it invites this retribution."
Second, the retribution received through the karma of the vehicles.
"First, those who do not awaken: when delusion reaches its extreme, they become desolate and run about without ceasing.
Second, those who do not remain deluded: once they attain awakening and awareness, it is suffering; they are scorched by immeasurable fires, and the pain is so profound it is difficult to endure."
Such are these perverse thoughts: when thoughts are bound together, they can become directions and locations;
when views are bound together, they can become mirrors and proofs;
when hearing is bound together, it can become massive boulders, ice, frost, earth, and mist.
When the breath is bound, it can become a great fire-chariot, a fire-boat, or a fire-cage;
when the flavor is bound, it can become a great cry of woe, remorse, or weeping;
when the touch is bound, it can become great or small, undergo ten thousand births and ten thousand deaths within a single day, or be turned face down or face up.
The objects of the mind’s focus—the two realms of arising and ceasing—further enable it to grasp objects through the five modes of clear perception (*vijñapti*).

When one is unaware, these are experienced as wildness, solitariness, and distraction; when one is not deluded, they are realized as suffering brought about by clarity. All of this occurs because of the karma created through perverse thoughts.
In this manner, one proceeds downward through the distinct locations of the sense organs;
these are the places where suffering is experienced.
"To examine" and "to verify" mean to provide evidence for one's prior transgressions.

This single faculty undergoes retribution, experiencing it through all the other faculties; yet, as the faculties encounter instruments of suffering, there are both disparities and correspondences, such that it is not necessarily the case that every faculty and its object are mutually concordant. Students should interpret this according to the text and must not harbor doubts or stagnate.
3. Conclusion and Manifestation of the Weighty Clarification, in three parts:
1. Concluding that it is illusory and false: "Ānanda!..."
"These are called the ten causes and six effects of hell; all are created by the deluded ignorance of sentient beings.
They create karma through delusion and receive retribution through delusion, all like flowers in the sky; yet, within cause and effect, there has never been any discrepancy.
2. Specifically revealing the gravity and lightness [of karma]:
"If various sentient beings collectively commit evil deeds, they enter the Avīci Hell and undergo immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas."

"When the six faculties and ten causes are fully present, they collectively create various karmas and enter the Avīci Hell; this refers to the Great Unquestioned [Hell] where five matters are fully present.
When each of the six faculties creates its own karma, and those actions involve both objects and faculties, such a person enters the Eight Uninterrupted Hells."

Just as the sixth consciousness, like the visual consciousness, takes only its own object and functions in conjunction with its respective faculty without involving other faculties, it does not possess the ten causes.

In this case, although all six faculties participate in the creation [of karma], at the time of creation they do not involve the other faculties; thus, upon entering the eight hot hells, the suffering is slightly lighter than before.
"If one commits the three acts of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct through body, speech, and mind, that person shall enter the eighteen hells.
Body, speech, and mind constitute three of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute three of the ten causes.

If one physically commits these three offenses—killing and so forth—while not committing them through speech or mind, and even if those latter acts are lighter than the former, one enters the eighteen hells.

"If one does not engage in all three types of karma simultaneously, but instead commits a single act of killing or a single act of stealing during the interim, such a person will enter thirty-six hells.
Thus, if one alone performs a single karma such as killing without engaging in other offenses, they enter thirty-six hells; furthermore, this is lighter than the previous case.
"If one sees with a single faculty and commits a single transgression, that person enters one hundred and eight hells.
This refers to committing only one act of killing with a single faculty; it is lighter than the previous case, yet still leads to entry into one hundred and eight hells.
If, within the sphere of one's intentions, there is improper reflection or wrong view that has not yet manifested in body or speech;
or if one kills a person through verbal action while the mind and body remain neutral (avyākṛta)—
these cases are all minor offenses.

Regarding the phrase "the seer of seeing": "seeing" (jiàn) is pronounced as xiàn; it refers exclusively to this single faculty and does not encompass the other faculties, hence it is called "the seer of seeing.
Third, this concludes the response to the question.
"Because sentient beings act and create individually, they enter the realm of homogeneity within the world; thus, their deluded imaginings arise, rather than existing from the beginning.
This is called 'individual creation' because, due to the non-interruption of the three karmas, each possesses their own private [karma]."

Because individual private karmas share a commonality, it is said that they "enter the stage of the same class" (*sabhāgabhūmi*). This means that through shared karma, beings collectively experience an undifferentiated commonality, whereas through distinct karma, each experiences a differentiated commonality; thus, the preceding text states: "Within the various classes of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), there are also the original stages."
All arise from the activation of false conceptualization; therefore, they are not inherently existent.
Second, the realm of hungry ghosts (preta-gati), which has three parts:
first, the general heading.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

These sentient beings have not violated the codes of discipline, nor transgressed the bodhisattva precepts, nor destroyed the Buddha’s nirvāṇa; yet, having been scorched by various other miscellaneous karmas throughout successive kalpas, they eventually exhaust their retribution and receive the forms of various hungry ghosts."
"One who breaks the disciplinary code slanders the existence of precepts;
one who violates the Bodhisattva precepts fails to restrain themselves regarding the gravity of offenses;
one who disparages the Buddha’s Nirvana does not believe in cause and effect."
These cases all involve the severance of the roots of goodness; other karmic consequences may be inferred accordingly.
Having been punished in hell for a long duration, it is said that they are scorched through successive kalpas.
Furthermore, having undergone other forms of rebirth, they enter the realm of hungry ghosts.
The ten classes of the realm of hungry ghosts arise from the aforementioned ten causes; the primary retributions for these ten causes have already been discussed in the preceding text.
Because they correspond to extreme suffering rather than being minor experiences, it is said that "only after their offenses are exhausted will they receive the forms of various hungry ghosts."
2. Specific Explanation:

"If, in a previous cause, one committed an offense out of greed for objects, that person, upon the completion of their retribution, encounters objects and takes form; this is called a 'strange ghost' (*piśāca*).
This is precisely the habit-energy of greed acting as the cause."

Having given rise to greed for objects and taking them through improper means, their remaining retribution lies among the hungry ghosts (preta), where they again take recourse in material things—namely, as spectral monsters of gold, silver, grasses, or trees; since these types are manifold, they are called "monster-ghosts" (kumbhāṇḍa).
"Currently undergoing the retribution of suffering in the Cold Ice Hell.
Having committed the offense of craving form, when this person’s transgression is exhausted, they encounter the wind and take shape, becoming what is called a *pāpaghna* (drought-demon) ghost.
This is due to the prior habituation to sexual desire serving as the cause.
Form can agitate and disorder the body and mind, like the wind blowing upon objects; it brings about rebirth in a ghostly form, which in turn relies upon the wind.
The nature of wind is fundamentally void, arising solely from habitual conditioning.
The correspondence between cause and effect is by no means in vain!
"When greed and delusion constitute an offense, once that person's retribution for the sin is exhausted, they encounter the form of an animal and are called a 'malignant ghost' (mei gui)."
This refers to the cause of having previously practiced deception.

Having established a foundation in falsehood and deluded by relying on the void, one takes refuge with animals and thus assumes a demonic form. Specifically, there are various species of foxes, wildcats, pigs, and dogs that possess extraordinary spirits; since these types are not limited to one, it is said that "one encounters an animal and forms [a spirit] accordingly."
The *mei* (demon) immediately manifests a beautiful form to delude people.
"When greed and resentment become offenses, once a person's retribution for those sins is exhausted, they encounter insects and take on their form; this is called the *gu-du* ghost."
This refers to the cause consisting of prior enmity and habitual tendencies.

Preceded by anger, one harbors malice without relinquishing it; the resentment is bound within the mind, and a burning affliction dwells in the heart. When receiving further retribution, one also assumes the form of poisonous species—namely, snakes, vipers, or venomous insects possessing spiritual agency—and becomes a *gudu* (poison-ghost).
"To harbor covetous recollections is a transgression. When such a person’s transgressions are exhausted, they encounter decline and take form as what is called a *pūtana* ghost.
This refers to the prior habituation to anger serving as the cause.

To dwell upon suffering and the instruments of suffering with hatred and resentment within one's heart, or to give rise to anger due to jealousy, and to not relinquish this angry resentment—this is called "covetous recollection."
When they receive their retribution as ghosts, they enter the bodies of those who encounter calamity and decline; these are called *lì-guǐ* (contagious ghosts).
Such things as toxic miasma, *shānghán* (epidemic fever), *chuánshī* (transmissible consumption), and *gùzhēng* (bone-steaming fever) are all produced by these ghosts.
"Greed and arrogance constitute offenses; when such a person has exhausted their karmic retribution, they encounter the vital energy (*qi*) and take form, being named a hungry ghost (*preta*).
This is precisely because their prior habituation to pride serves as the cause.
Arrogance involves looking down upon others and treating things with disdain, holding oneself aloft and asserting one's own strength."

As for those who report to the realm of ghosts, they take on form through the meeting of vital energies; yet, lacking internal substance and virtue, they remain empty-bellied while harboring loftiness of mind. Because they are tormented by hunger, they are called *preta*, or "hungry ghosts."

"Deceitful greed constitutes a transgression; when this person’s retribution for their sins is exhausted, they encounter the realm of obscurity and take on a form known as a 'demon of nightmares' (yān-guǐ).
This is precisely because their prior habit of deception serves as the cause.

To gain profit and reputation, they harbor many heterodox schemes, feigning the possession of virtue while deceiving others, causing them to remain in darkness and ignorance regarding their own affairs."
Having received the form of a ghost, they rely on the profound and entrust themselves to the dark; they bewilder and delude those who sleep, and are therefore called *yān-guǐ* (sleep-demon ghosts).
Because their transgression was greed for light, when this person’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter a *jing* (essence-spirit) and take its form, being called *wǎngliǎng-guǐ* (mantis-ghosts).
This refers to seeing habitual tendencies as the cause.
Clinging to views, ordinary beings each claim their own clear realization; their births are mutually opposed, and they give rise to defiance.

This leads them to summon the realm of ghosts, where they encounter places of refined spirit and take on form—reposing their substance in the essence and radiance of the sun and moon, or in the brilliant spirits of mountains and marshes.
As for what are called *wangliang*, they are transformations and anomalies of water and stone.

"When greed becomes a transgression, once that person's retribution for their sins is exhausted, they encounter a manifestation of light and take on form; this is termed a 'ghost employed as a servant.'"
This refers precisely to the cause of habitual conditioning (*vāsanā*).
By suppressing and stripping away [the truth], and by fabricating structures based on emptiness, one exerts the mind and employs thought to afflict the innocent and render them guilty.
When encountering manifest objects, they rely upon them to form their bodies; they are not of the obscure or dark class.
Because they serve as messengers on battlefields and are among those who carry sand and shoulder stones, they are called "servants."

"To form factions out of greed is a transgression; when such a person's retribution for that sin is exhausted, they encounter humans and take on a physical form, being called a *shouzhuang gui* (a 'conveying ghost').
This refers to the habit of litigation as the cause.

To side with oneself and conceal one's crimes, only to be sued by others, results in rebirth among the class of ghosts. Taking up a substance within the human realm—such as those in the world known as child-tutors (*tongzi shi*) or shamans and invocators (*wuzhu*)—who all convey words concerning the auspicious or inauspicious, the calamitous or fortunate, from the realm of spirits, they are called *shouzhuang gui*.
The classes of ghosts above this are indeed numerous; yet, when examining their effects and tracing their causes, they do not exceed these ten.
Third, the concluding summary: "Ānanda!..."
These people all fall due to their pure passions; once the fires of karma have burned them dry, they emerge above as ghosts.
All such beings are summoned by the karma of their own deluded thoughts; yet if one awakens to Bodhi, then the wondrous, perfect, and luminous nature is fundamentally nothing at all.
"The ten causes and six retributions are all produced by pure emotion (*qing*). Since emotion has already sunk downward, one consequently falls into hell.
After undergoing long treatment in hell, when emotion is exhausted, one ascends; thus it is said that once the fires of karma have burned everything dry, one emerges above as a ghost."
The mind of a ghost is light and restless, a remnant of the fires of karma; it is summoned by one's own deluded karma and cannot be obtained from another.
Within the mind of Bodhi, all are like flowers in the sky.
3. The animal realm has three parts:
first, the general statement:
"Furthermore, Ānanda!"

Once the karma of the ghost realm is exhausted, both emotion and thought become empty; only then, encountering the person to whom one originally owed a debt in the world, does one take birth as an animal to repay that karmic debt from former lives.
In the hells, one is disciplined through emotion; among ghosts, one is disciplined through perception. When emotion and perception are exhausted, it is said that emptiness is realized.
However, that which is emptied is precisely the karma generated based upon emotion and perception.
Once the karma of the two paths has perished, one returns to the realm of animals to repay former debts, using the lives of camels, donkeys, oxen, and horses to compensate others.
If one is among other species, one receives retribution accordingly.
2. Specific Explanation:
"The ghosts of material anomalies, once their material substance has dissolved and their retribution is exhausted, are born into the human world, mostly as the class of owls (*xiāo*).
Those who habitually practiced greed become anomaly-ghosts; when their retribution is exhausted, they are reborn among the species of owls."
The *xiāo* is the earth-owl (*tǔxiāo*). It forms its young by attaching soil clods; this is caused by greed for material things. All manner of strange anomalies are subsumed under this category.

"The ghosts of the *fēngbò* (wind-demoness) are born into the world when their karmic retribution from the wind-spirits is exhausted; they mostly manifest as portents of calamity and all kinds of heterodox phenomena."

With the habitual practice of lust as the cause, one invites the retribution of wind-demons and drought spirits; as a secondary consequence, one undergoes the signs of retribution among the animal realm.
"Guo" (咎) means transgression or evil;
"zheng" (徵) means a responsive omen or verification.
That which is summoned by evil conduct will bring about calamities and anomalies; these portents appear beforehand.

For instance, flocks of sparrows and swarms of rats are omens of famine; the *jiaoyu* bird foretells floods, while the dancing of cranes indicates abundant droughts—such examples are not limited to these alone.
"Those ghosts who possessed animals, once their retribution for possessing the dead is exhausted, are reborn in this world, mostly as foxes.
Due to the karmic retribution of their deceitful causes, they became ghosts and then spirits; when that basis is exhausted, they receive the body of a fox."
"The ghosts of insect-inflicted *gū* (poisonous charms) perish when their retribution is exhausted and are reborn in the world, mostly as species of venomous creatures.
As a retribution for the habituation of resentment, these ghosts manifest as *gū*-poisons, and animals become venomous species, such as the *luán* (viper), snakes, *fù* (vipers), and scorpions."
"Demons of decay and pestilence—those born into this world as a retribution for their exhaustion and decline—are mostly of the class of worms.

Due to the cause of habitual anger, these demons become agents of decay and pestilence; they entrust themselves to calamities and attach to misfortunes, entering into the body. They subsequently take animal forms and again lodge within the body, becoming intestinal worms and pinworms.
"Those ghosts who received [human] breath, once their vital energy has dissolved and their retribution is exhausted, are born into the world, mostly as types of food.

Hungry ghosts attach themselves to breath; arrogance and habituation are the causes. These ghosts suffer from hunger and emptiness, while animals satisfy the fullness of others; thus they become 'types of food,' namely those animals in the world that may be eaten."
"Souls of those who died in obscurity, having exhausted their retributions in the dark realm, are mostly reborn as domestic animals.

Due to the habitual tendencies of past causes, they become ghosts that cause nightmares; once these have dissolved, they are reborn as domestic animals—such as donkeys, oxen, horses, and silkworm cocoons—to be used for human service."
"Coarse" (mian) refers to being dense and not clearly manifest.
"The ghosts of refined essence," having dissolved their harmony and exhausted their retribution, are born into the world; they mostly become responsive manifestations.

Because they have seen and practiced [such things], the ghosts manifest as *wangliang* spirits; once their radiant essence is exhausted, they become animals according to their kind, appearing at the appropriate times of the year and season to call out again.
What is called "harmony" (he) is a mixture; it is through the mingling of the refined and brilliant that one becomes a ghost.
When the brilliance of a spiritual being fades and its retribution is exhausted, it is born into the world, often appearing as auspicious omens for all classes of beings.

This refers to past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): a ghost (*preta*) manifests through the clarity of one's consciousness and becomes a type of servile spirit. When the karma of the ghost realm is exhausted, the retribution of the animal realm ceases.

"Cessation" (*xiū*) means "beauty"; as auspicious signs are about to arrive, these omens appear in advance. They are summoned by the beauty of another's virtuous conduct, such as the appearance of the *qilin* and the *phoenix*.
"Those ghosts who depend on humans, when the person dies and their retribution is exhausted, are reborn in the world; for the most part, they follow their own kind.

Due to the causes of habitual litigation, ghosts summon and transmit them; when a person dies and becomes an animal, the retribution lies in their sharp intelligence, hence they are said to 'follow their own kind.'"
That is to say, those creatures that are domesticated and compliant with human beings.
Third, the conclusion and indication, in two parts:
first, the formal conclusion regarding their falsity.

“Ānanda! These beings all have their karmic debts exhausted by the fire of karma, which withers them dry; they are reborn as animals as a consequence. All of these, too, are summoned and led forth by their own deluded karma. If they were to awaken to Bodhi, then these delusive conditions would fundamentally not exist.”

In the two realms of hell-beings and hungry ghosts, once they have been completely consumed by the fires of karma and their emotional and conceptual faculties have withered away, they now undergo rebirth as animals to repay their remaining karmic debts; therefore, it is said that they "turn sideways."

They exist because of deluded thoughts, yet the awakened nature is fundamentally non-existent; they are like circular shadows seen due to the ailment of cataracts. Second, the question is cited to provide further clarification:

"As you have said regarding Jewel-Lotus Fragrance and others, as well as King Vairatya and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra—such evil karma was originally manifested by themselves; it did not descend from heaven, nor emerge from the earth, nor was it given by others. It was summoned by their own delusions and must be experienced by themselves. Within the mind of Bodhi, these are all merely floating and empty, being the solidification of deluded thoughts."

Regarding the three conditions you asked about: these are produced by the false karmic actions created by each individual; they do not arise from another. Therefore, it is said that they are fundamentally not bestowed from heaven, and so forth.

Delusory creation and delusory reception are, within the nature of awakening, all like flowers in the sky. 1. Repayment of Excess Reckonings.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
When these beings from the animal realm repay their prior debts, if the debtor repays more than what was owed, these sentient beings will again become human and must repay the excess."

"Exceeding one's portion" means to go beyond one's allotted share; it refers to acting in excess without adhering to one's proper measure, such as performing unreasonable forced labor regardless of its severity, or working without rest day or night, or consuming food without moderation.
All such categories as these ought to be subject to a counter-investigation regarding their surplus.

Now there are those who, relying on their nobility, act with license; leaning on their power and influence, they live in extravagance; coveting their labor, they impose heavy service; seizing their flesh for flavor, they kill them unjustly. Morning and evening they do not cease, taking no account of their toil and suffering. When their merit is exhausted, they must face this reckoning of their surplus—how fitting it is that this should happen!
"If they possess both power and merit, they shall repay that power among human beings without relinquishing their human form.
If they lack merit, they shall instead become animals to repay the remaining balance."
"Those who cultivate goodness and honor merit receive their recompense for such efforts within this very human body.

Now we observe that households of accumulated virtue often see their wealth greatly depleted—whether by robbery, by debts, by being subjected to forced labor, or by unjustly receiving beatings. All of these are the result of past karma; having exhausted the retribution for this life, they must repay the remainder as animals. Because they cultivated merit, they have received a partial repayment among humans; had they not been so, they would surely have become animals.
Thus, it is clear that those who lack goodness [do not even attain this human state]."
Second, the difficulty of exhausting the cycle of retribution:
"Ānanda, you should know that if one uses another's wealth or labor, the obligation ceases once it has been fully repaid.

However, if in the interim one takes another's life or eats their flesh, then for as many *rajas* (dust-motes) eons as there are grains of sand, they will continue to devour and slaughter one another."
"It is like a turning wheel that alternates between rising and falling without rest; it cannot be halted except through *śamatha* or the appearance of a Buddha in the world.

You owe another wealth, while another owes you labor; now that the debt has been repaid, it ceases of its own accord once the repayment is complete. The worldly tending of oxen and horses is of this same nature.

If one were to kill another as before and eat their flesh, this would instead constitute the karma of killing; body taking body and life repaying life, as humans eat sheep and sheep die to become humans, they would come to accuse one another in turn without end.
Among all karmas, the taking of life is the most grave; if one does not encounter the appearance of a Buddha and cultivate *śamatha*, it can never be extinguished.
Second, the specific explanation:
"You should now know that those of the owl species, having received their full retribution and returned to human form, are born into the human realm as members of the dull and stubborn class."
"Because of their greed for objects, ghosts assume strange forms, and animals such as earth-owls nourish themselves by clutching clods of soil.

Now that they have returned to the human realm, their natures remain dull and ignorant; they are mixed among the stubborn and the foolish, and their minds forget virtue and righteousness—it is precisely because of these past causes that this is so."

As for what is called "convergence," when human beings receive retribution according to the Way, it is summoned by virtuous causes; although the general retribution is the same, the completing karmas (*pūrṇakarma*) differ, and thus they are divided into ten types.

Now, those who come from among the animals receive this as a secondary consequence of residual karma; it is not summoned by primary wholesome karma, yet it is still induced by subsequent karma. Because it is not upright, it is said to be "intermingled"; others are all to be understood in this same way.
"When those portents of retribution have been fully requited and their forms restored, they are reborn among human beings, joining the ranks of the ignorant.
Originally caused by greed and desire, the ghosts assumed the forms of drought-demons (*pāpa*); this was the response to the calamities of the animal realm."

When their karma is exhausted, they return to their original state and join the ranks of the foolish; because those with excessive desire do not practice distinct virtues but instead focus exclusively on a single object, their failure to cultivate virtue results in the induction of dullness and stupidity.
Regarding the distinction between the stubborn and the ignorant: "stubborn" refers to one who knows what is good but does not follow it, and who refuses to receive instruction.
"Ignorant" refers to one who is shrouded in darkness and whose consciousness is dull and difficult to enlighten; this is the difference between them.
“Those of the fox lineage, having received their retribution and returned to human form, are born among the human race as members of a perverse class.
Because they follow the habits of deceit, ghosts become animal-demons; such beings enter the category of animals, being subsumed within the class of foxes.”
Now, having entered the human realm, he is among those who are perverse, stubborn, and self-opinionated, refusing to accept admonition or instruction.
"Those of such poisonous character, having received their full retribution and returned to physical form, are born into the human path, mingling with the common and mediocre."
The habit-energy of resentment is the cause; ghosts act as the malevolent poisons, while serpents and scorpions among the beasts are their manifested forms.
When they return to the human realm, they are born among the common masses—specifically those of vulgar and base character whose natures are coarse and impulsive.
"Those belonging to the class of worms, having received their retribution and regained their physical forms, are born into the human realm as minute creatures.

With the habit of anger as the cause, they dwell among ghosts as sources of decay and pestilence; as parasitic worms, they receive the status of lowly animals. Even when they become humans, they are not even recorded among the ranks of humanity."
"Those who consume the collective merit are rewarded with sufficient sustenance that restores their forms; they are reborn among the human path, joining the ranks of sentient beings.
Arrogance is the cause [of their state]; they summon hunger as ghosts, forming through the binding of vital breaths without substantial reality, receiving food as animals do."
That humans are weak and yielding is largely due to their arrogance and pride, which instead invite the retribution of timidity and cowardice.
Those who have served their fellow beings receive a full recompense in the form of rebirth; born into the human realm, they are integrated among those subject to toil and labor.
With the habit of deception as the cause, one becomes a ghost who follows from the dark realm of nightmares, or an animal for the sake of clothing and service.
As a human, one undergoes toil and labor, engaging in the hardships of manual service and the various arts of craftsmanship.
"Those who correspond to the human category shall receive sufficient recompense and restore their physical forms, being born into the human realm to participate in the ranks of the civilized.

Because of their subsequent habits and perceptions, they may fall as ghosts or spirits; when their retribution as *wangliang* demons ends, they shall be reborn as animals according to the timing of their karma."
Participating in the human realm with a slight degree of refinement and culture, yet not being a direct cause for cultivation, it is therefore called "participatory integration" (*sancha*).
As for those who possess auspicious signs, their retribution is fulfilled and they take form again, born within the human realm as members of the enlightened class through participatory integration.

Habitual practice constitutes karma; when one receives the spirit of a ghost, one is driven and dispatched at a rapid pace, with no moment’s rest. When one invites the response of an animal, one is reborn as such.
Humans possess a mixture of intelligence; when examining the fruit, it follows from its cause, without any deviation whatsoever.
"Those who have fulfilled their karmic obligations and regained their physical forms are reborn among human beings, joining the ranks of the enlightened.

Because of their past habituation to litigation, ghosts take up residence within humans; they transmit divine utterances to reveal fortune and calamity, and through training, they become clever and docile."
When a person reaches the point of ultimate understanding, they are unperturbed by honor or disgrace and remain at ease with themselves; therefore, they are called those of the "enlightened" class.
Third, the conclusion and indication: "Ānanda!..."

All these have now fully repaid their past debts and have again taken human form; yet, due to the inverted bonds of karma from beginningless time, they have continued to give birth to one another and kill one another. Having failed to encounter the Tathāgata or hear the True Dharma, they naturally revolve within the midst of worldly afflictions; such people as these are called those who are to be pitied.

In the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals, they repay their prior karma; once the retributions of the three miserable paths are exhausted, they return to human form, drawn by subsequent wholesome karma. Within this state, they are further divided into ten distinct categories, all of which constitute the inverted cycle of transmigration.
To cease these inversions, there is only morality, concentration, and wisdom; without these three, one will not cease the cycle of saṃsāra.
If the Buddha had not appeared in the world, who would have taught this Dharma for them to practice and study, so as to escape from saṃsāra?
5. The Realm of the Rishis (ṛṣigati), in two parts:
first, the general heading. "Ānanda!..."

Furthermore, there are followers who do not rely on the Perfect Enlightenment to cultivate samādhi, but instead separately cultivate deluded thoughts, maintaining their mental conceptions to preserve their physical forms. They roam in mountain forests and remote places inaccessible to ordinary people; these are the ten kinds of immortals (ṛṣis).

Regarding "not relying on the Perfectly Awakened One": the practices of the Three Vehicles are all taught by the Buddha; yet even this present sutra rebukes those of the Two Vehicles, stating that they do not recognize the root of birth and death and practice in a confused manner—how much more so for those who would cultivate the Way of the Immortals!
"Maintaining visualization to solidify the form" means fixing the mind on longevity and immortality so that this physical body becomes firm and indestructible.
"Cultivating separate deluded thoughts" refers to the ten methods of refinement described below.

All of these possess outflows (*sāsrava*); they are superior to humans in their decline yet inferior to devas in their progress. Because they dwell in mountain forests in places inaccessible to ordinary people, this is called the realm of the *ṛṣis* (*ṛṣigati*).
However, this single realm does not appear in other sūtras, as its collective retribution is identical to that of humans.

As for those currently mentioned in this sutra, they are categorized as such because their specific practices differ from the path; furthermore, since they are not subsumed under the two destinies of humans and devas, they are all classified among the ranks of externalists (*tīrthika*).

Nevertheless, these practices prohibit what is not the Buddha’s true precepts; they merely forbid coarse and superficial matters, which constitutes the "clinging to rules and observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
2. Specific Manifestation.
"Ānanda! Those sentient beings who take medicinal elixirs with steadfast persistence without ceasing, until the path of food is perfected, are called earth-walking immortals (bhūmicara-rṣi)."

As for those who take medicinal herbs, they consume hemp seeds and the fruits of plants and trees; they preserve their physical forms for a long duration, and their lifespans extend over a full kalpa. Yet, they are not yet able to achieve levitation. When this path is perfected, they are called earth-walking immortals (*bhūcarī-ṛṣi*).
"Remaining firm as grasses and trees without ceasing, when the Way of Medicine is perfected, one is called a Flying Immortal.
"Grasses and trees" refers to those who consume pine and eat cypress, and the like.
Because grasses and trees are light, their substance becomes light when consumed; consequently, one flies through the air without falling to the ground.
Remaining steadfast as metal or stone without ceasing until the Way of transformation is perfected, such a person is called a "Wandering Immortal" (Cāraṇa-ṛṣi).
"Metals and stones" refers to such things as the ingestion of cinnabar to achieve the "nine transformations.
There are two kinds of transformation:
first, it can transform the bones so that one’s lifespan is prolonged and the body remains upright; second, it can transform material objects so that the base becomes noble.
If this path is perfected, one may roam at will among humans, relieving poverty and alleviating suffering with sovereign ease.
When one’s movements and stillness are firm and unwavering, and the vital energy (*prāṇa*) and essence are fully perfected, one is called an *ākāśagāmin* (Space-Traveling Immortal).

By regulating and nourishing harmony, and employing it to circulate the vital energies (rō-ei), one’s spirit and breath remain long-established, enabling one to walk upon the void; when this efficacy is perfected, the body becomes firm and longevity eternal—this is called "walking in the void" (kūgyō).
"Solidifying the vital fluids without ceasing, one brings the virtue of moisture to perfect completion; this is called the 'Heavenly-Walking Immortal' (Tianxingxian).
By drumming the celestial pond, swallowing the vital fluids, and consolidating the essence, after a long period the merit becomes manifest, and one thus achieves the virtue of moisture."

As for what is called the "heavenly path" (devayāna), this does not refer to the six heavens of desire; rather, it refers to what worldly people call "heaven," meaning the abodes of numinous immortals (ṛṣis), such as when Zhang Qian sought the source of the Yellow River and reached Mount Kunlun, where he beheld celestial palaces and the like.
Alternatively, because their conduct does not engage with the realm of desire and is no different from that of the devas, it is called "deva-conduct" (*devacara*).
When the essence and color are firm and stable without ceasing, and one inhales the refined purity to achieve perfection, this is called "the practice of the siddha" (*siddhacara*).

By ingesting the vital essence of the sun and moon and focusing the mind on transformative cultivation to prolong their physical lives, they eventually achieved extraordinary insights through long-term practice; thus, they were able to comprehend the sentiments and conditions of the world, which is why they are called "those who possess universal penetration."
"By practicing incantations and prohibitions (*dhāraṇī-vidhi*) without ceasing, one brings the methods of the arts to perfection; such a person is called a 'Path-Walking Immortal' (*caryā-siddha*).

Incantations and prohibitions are precisely the methods and arts of the immortals; by means of these, one sustains the body, prolonging and fortifying it. When the power of these arts is accomplished, it is termed "Path-Walking."
"Steadfastly maintaining mindfulness without ceasing, until the recollection is fully perfected, this is called the 'Illuminating Practice Immortal.

One contemplates the preceding object, binding the mind so as not to forget, focusing intently without shifting; after a long time, its function manifests, illuminating the realm and comprehending the source of all transformations. Because it is like wisdom arising from meditative concentration, it is named 'Illuminating Practice.'"
"Solidly joined and intermingling without ceasing, when the resonance and response are perfectly accomplished, this is called a 'Refined-Practice Immortal' (jingxing xian).

In the world there are arts of 'gathering yin' and 'gathering yang,' which are termed 'intermingling. After long practice, success is achieved; through this mutual resonance and response, one inhales the vital essence of the other to consolidate one's own body, and is therefore called 'Refined Practice'."
"Steadfastly manifesting transformations without ceasing, awakening to perfect realization—this is called the Immortal of Transcendent Conduct.
Contemplating that all things in the world are transformations, once the objective realm has been transformed, the mental conceptions also vanish, becoming like withered wood.
Because conditioned effort can only achieve such results for a brief moment, it is said that "activity is severed.

As for why all ten categories mentioned above are referred to as "practitioners" (xingzhe), it is because through long-term cultivation, they have achieved mastery and their realization has flowed forth universally.
3. Conclusion and Demonstration: "Ānanda!

These individuals all refine their minds among human beings, yet they do not cultivate true awakening; instead, they attain a distinct mode of existence, living for ten million years, dwelling in deep mountains or on large ocean islands, far removed from the realm of humanity."

"This, too, is the wandering and revolving of deluded thoughts within saṃsāra; failing to cultivate samādhi, one returns once the retribution is exhausted, scattering into the various realms of existence.
The "principle of life" refers to the principle of longevity, which is precisely the ten methods of cultivation and refinement mentioned above.

Regarding the term "among humans," since there is no distinct collective retribution for the realm of immortals (*ṛṣi*), one becomes an immortal by adding the ten preceding modes of cultivation and refinement to the fruit of the collective retribution of the human body itself.

Deluded thoughts are not true; in the end, one follows karma and falls. (The first section follows: [1] Enumeration of the heavens. Three: [1] Enumeration
First, the Desire Realm, has two parts:
first, the enumeration and explanation, which has six sections;
first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.

“Ānanda! Those people in the world who do not seek the permanent abode, yet are unable to abandon the affectionate attachments to their wives and concubines, remain free from the flow of lustful thoughts toward sexual misconduct; their minds become clear and luminous, and after the end of their lives, they shall dwell near the sun and the moon.”
"Such a class of beings is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Because they do not seek permanence, they do not cultivate right awakening.

Due to the absence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they cannot relinquish craving; yet, because they possess virtuous precepts (*śīla*), their minds do not wander or dissipate, and by the power of their roots of goodness, their minds are clear and their bodies luminous.
This clarifies and purifies the desirous mind, giving rise to the nature of luminosity.
When such a person’s life ends, they will be reborn on the midpoint of Mount Sumeru, adjacent to the palaces of the sun and moon; all the celestial hosts there are governed by this heaven.
2. The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

"Their sensual desire for their own wives and harems is slight; while they dwell in the Pure Abodes, they do not obtain full flavor [of sensory experience]. After the end of their lives, they transcend the brilliance of the sun and moon and dwell at the summit of the human realm."
"Such a class of beings is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
As their craving for sensual desire gradually diminishes, their attachment even to their own households and families decreases; therefore, they do not experience full flavor.
"Flavor" (rasa) here means attachment.
Regarding the term "Pure Abodes" (*śuddhāvāsa*): they are so called because they are not produced by impurity, thereby distinguishing them from those who practice deviance.
As for "surpassing the sun and moon": this is because their goodness increases;
as their attachment to desire further diminishes and their bodies ascend once more, they are thus born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—here translated as "Thirty-three"—is the abode of Śakra.
Third is the Yāma Heaven.

When encountering desire, they engage with it briefly, and upon its departure, they have no lingering thoughts. In the human world, their movement is slight and their stillness is great; after the end of life, they dwell serenely in the midst of space. The light of the sun and moon cannot shine upward there, for these beings possess their own radiance.
"Such a class is called the Suyāma Heaven.

Because they have not yet abandoned the mind of desire, they encounter objects only briefly; as their attachment to the lower realm gradually thins, it is said that they depart without further thought or recollection.
When encountering desire, one still engages with it, and thus it is said that movement is slight;
when free from such thoughts and recollections, it is said that stillness predominates.
As this practice increases and the body becomes further refined, the stage of birth is reached.
Yama is the Cloud of Time; this is the first heaven among those dwelling in space.
Fourth is Tuṣita Heaven. It is "always tranquil";

even when sensory contacts arise, they cannot cause disturbance. After life ends, one ascends to a state of subtle refinement, no longer descending to the realms of humans or devas in the lower worlds, and remains beyond the reach of the three calamities that destroy the kalpa.
"Such a class [of beings] is called the Tuṣita Heaven.
Because their practice is superior to that of the former, it is said that they are "tranquil at all times.
Regarding "that which should be contacted" (*spraṣṭavya*): "should" (*spraṣṭavya*) means "corresponding," and "contacted" (*spraṣṭavya*) refers to the objects of desire.
Because they still comply with and follow [the world], it is said that they have not yet been able to contravene it.
As their lives draw to a close, they gradually become superior and are thus born in this heaven.

Regarding the phrase "ascending to the refined and subtle," this refers to the vessel-world (bhājanaloka) where Bodhisattvas in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha) reside; because it shares the same name as Tuṣita, it is here called "Contentment" (Tuṣita).
5. The Heaven of Delighting in Transformations:

"I have no lustful mind; I act in accordance with your conduct, yet when you lie across me, my experience is like chewing wax. After my life ends, I shall be reborn in the Land of Transformation Beyond."
"Thus, this class is called the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations.

When the mind has no intentionality toward objects, objects come forth spontaneously; since the objects themselves possess [the capacity for] mental engagement, what flavor can the self find therein? Therefore, it is said that their enjoyment is like chewing wax and so forth.

Because they enjoy the objects of the five desires through their own power of transformation, [they are called] the Sixth, the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
"They possess no worldly mind, yet they perform actions identical to those of the world."

In their conduct and interactions, they clearly transcend [all limitations]; after the end of life, they are universally able to emerge and transcend, manifesting both transformed and non-transformed realms.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
"Regarding 'the activities and interactions,' this is also a horizontal presentation.
Although there was previously a lack of flavor, the mind still gave rise to desire when encountering objects.
This, however, is a state of no-mind; therefore, it is said that one clearly transcends."

However, for now, let us speak in terms of the absence of coarse characteristics; yet how could subtle craving and desire be absent, since they have not yet transcended the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*)?
As for "those who create" and "those who do not create": "those who create" refers to the fifth heaven (*nirmāṇarati*), while "those who do not create" refers to the various heavens below it.

The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Because they enjoy the five objects of desire manifested by others, and because they possess the sovereign power to command those manifestations for their own enjoyment, they are called 'Masters over Others' Emanations' (*paranirmitavaśavartin*)."

"In the six heavens above, as the mind of desire gradually lightens, the retribution obtained becomes progressively superior; those whose passions are heavy will certainly not be reborn in these heavens.
As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The six [heavens] experience desire through embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing."
This also clarifies the minor characteristics of accepting sensual desires.
Second, the conclusion and demonstration: “Ānanda!
"Thus, although the forms of these six heavens have transcended [the earth], their mental traces still intersect; from this point downward, they are called the Realm of Desire.

These six heavens possess bodily radiance, can travel through the air with ease, and enjoy long lifespans that gradually increase and improve, differing from the human realms below; therefore, it is said that "although their forms have transcended [the earth]."

Furthermore, the various classes of beings within the human realm have short lifespans and are subject to constant change and instability; by contrast, the merit and life-span of the heavens are generally difficult to disturb, which is why it is said they "move forth.
Yet, because they still encounter the realms of desire, it is said that "the mind and its traces still intersect."
If one reaches the stage of meditative concentration (*samāpatti-bhūmi*), there will forever be no opposition from desire.
*Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra Commentary*, Fascicle Eight, Part Three.
